'''Braun''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Carol Moseley Braun]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Peter Fitzgerald (politician)|Peter Fitzgerald]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 50.25% }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''1998 United States Senate election in Illinois''' was held November 3, 1998. Democratic incumbent [[Carol Moseley Braun]] ran for re-election to a second term in office but was defeated by Republican state senator Peter Fitzgerald. In the Republican primary election, Fitzgerald narrowly defeated state comptroller [[Loleta Didrickson]]. Braun was unopposed. In the primary elections, turnout was 20.55% with 1,386,694 total votes cast.{{cite web |title=Voter Turnout |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/VoterTurnout.aspx?MID=fVf30XCcBCY%3d&T=637204877664537563 |website=www.elections.il.gov |publisher=Illinois State Board of Elections |access-date=22 March 2020 |archive-date=August 26, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250826050848/https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/VoterTurnout.aspx?MID=fVf30XCcBCY%3D&T=637204877664537563 |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |title=Election Results |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/ElectionVoteTotals.aspx |website=www.elections.il.gov |publisher=Illinois State Board of Elections |access-date=23 March 2020 |archive-date=22 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200222093629/https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/ElectionVoteTotals.aspx |url-status=dead }} In the general election, Braun was dogged by a series of controversies which had marred her first term in office, and Fitzgerald led in most public opinion polling, often by a large margin. However, Braun closed the gap late in the campaign by appealing to African American voters. On Election Day, Braun won a large majority of the vote in [[Cook County, Illinois|Cook County]], beating polling by several points, but Fitzgerald won the race by a surprisingly close margin. Fitzgerald was the only Republican candidate to defeat an incumbent Democratic senator in 1998. == Background == During Moseley Braun's first term as U.S. senator, she was plagued by several major controversies. In 1993, she was the subject of a [[Federal Election Commission]] investigation over $249,000 in unaccounted campaign funds. The commission found that Braun had violated [[campaign finance]] law but took no action, citing a lack of resources. Moseley Braun admitted only to bookkeeping errors. The [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] turned down two requests by the [[Internal Revenue Service]] to investigate.''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'', [http://www.slate.com/id/2078924/ Is Carol Moseley-Braun a Crook?"], February 19, 2003 In 1996, Moseley Braun made a private trip to [[Nigeria]], where she met with military dictator [[Sani Abacha]]. Despite U.S. [[economic sanctions|sanctions]] against the country and Abacha, the senator did not notify nor register her trip with the [[United States Department of State]]. She subsequently defended Abacha's human rights record in Congress.''[[NPR]]'', [https://www.npr.org/programs/specials/democrats2004/braun.html "2004 Democratic Presidential Candidates: Carol Moseley Braun"], Npr.org, May 6, 2003 == Democratic primary == === Candidates === * [[Carol Moseley Braun]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1993 === Results === {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Carol Moseley Braun]] (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 666,419 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 666,419 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} == Republican primary == === Candidates === * [[Loleta Didrickson]], [[Illinois comptroller]] * [[Peter Fitzgerald (politician)|Peter Fitzgerald]], state senator from [[Inverness, Illinois|Inverness]] === Campaign === Fitzgerald, a multimillionaire, spent nearly $7 million in the Republican primary.{{cite web|url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/access/27530977.html?dids=27530977:27530977&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Mar+19%2C+1998&author=Jon+Jeter&pub=The+Washington+Post&desc=Moseley-Braun%27s+Rich+Foe+May+Be+Surprisingly+Strong&pqatl=google |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120714231350/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/access/27530977.html?dids=27530977:27530977&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Mar+19,+1998&author=Jon+Jeter&pub=The+Washington+Post&desc=Moseley-Braun's+Rich+Foe+May+Be+Surprisingly+Strong&pqatl=google |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 14, 2012 |title=Moseley-Braun's Rich Foe May Be Surprisingly Strong |publisher=Pqasb.pqarchiver.com |date=March 19, 1998 |access-date=April 4, 2015}} === Results === Fitzgerald won the Republican primary with 51.8% of the vote to Didrickson's 48.2%.[http://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionResults.aspx?ID=ja0yDQ6QgdA%3d Election Results: General Primary - Torgersen (Reform) === Campaign === In September, Moseley Braun created controversy again by using the racial slur "[[nigger]]" in describing her own experiences with racism.{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-senator-apologizes-for-e/158021325/ |title=Senator Apologizes For Epithet Moseley-Braun Uses Slur In Calling Columnist Racist |first1=Rick |last1=Pearson |first2=Graeme |last2=Zielinski |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |pages=1, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-senator-apologizes-for-e/158021449/ 7] |date=September 8, 1998 |access-date=April 4, 2015}} Most polls over the first few months showed Moseley-Braun trailing badly. However, after she was helped in the final month by notable Democrats such as [[First Lady of the United States|first lady]] [[Hillary Clinton]] and U.S. Representative [[Luis Gutiérrez]], three polls published in the last week showed her within the margin of error, and, in one poll, running even with Fitzgerald.{{cite news |last=Belluck |first=Pam |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/03/us/the-1998-campaign-illinois-moseley-braun-trailing-pushes-hard.html?pagewanted=1 |title=The 1998 Campaign – Illinois – Moseley-Braun, Trailing, Pushes Hard |location=Illinois |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=A23 |date=November 3, 1998 |access-date=April 4, 2015 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250622040753/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/03/us/the-1998-campaign-illinois-moseley-braun-trailing-pushes-hard.html |archive-date=22 June 2025 |url-status=live}} Between the primary and general election, Fitzgerald spent over $12 million in total on the two races. ===Polling=== {| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%;text-align:center;" |- valign=bottom ! |{{party shading/Democratic}}|'''41%''' |35% |24% |} === Results === Moseley Braun was narrowly defeated, winning only five of Illinois's 102 counties. However, the race was much closer than expected, thanks to Moseley Braun's massive margin in [[Cook County, Illinois|Cook County]] and the city of [[Chicago]]. For the general election, turnout was 50.25%, with 3,394,521 votes cast.{{cite web |title=Voter Turnout |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/VoterTurnout.aspx?MID=fVf30XCcBCY%3d&T=637204879738085590 |website=www.elections.il.gov |publisher=Illinois State Board of Elections |access-date=22 March 2020 |archive-date=May 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250502212157/https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/VoterTurnout.aspx?MID=fVf30XCcBCY%3D&T=637204879738085590 |url-status=dead }} As of 2026, this was one of five elections in the past eight midterm cycles, since [[1990 United States House of Representatives elections|1990]], to involve the incumbent president's party losing a Senate seat in a state that leaned more than 10 points towards them in the preceding presidential election. The other races were the [[2006 United States Senate election in Montana]], the [[2010 United States Senate election in Illinois]], the [[2010 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania]], and the [[2010 United States Senate election in Wisconsin]].{{Cite tweet |last=Klein |first=Matthew |user=MattKleinOnline |number=2117099265579446701 |date=November 1, 2026 |title=To win the Senate, Democrats must flip seats in states the president carried by double digits two years before. How often does that happen? Answer: Not often — only five times throughout all the midterms since 1990!
